source.title: Asymmetries in explosive strength following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction

paper.citation: Knezevic, O. M., Mirkov, D. M., Kadija, M., Nedeljkovic, A., & Jaric, S. (2014). Asymmetries in explosive strength following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The Knee, 21(6), 1039–1045. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knee.2014.07.021
paper.abstract: How do quadriceps and hamstring maximal-force and rate-of-force-development asymmetries change from pre-ACLR to four and six months post-ACLR? Twenty male athletes with ACL injury tested before reconstruction and at four and six months afterward. Heterogeneous athletic backgrounds; no women. Single-joint isometric testing rather than sport-specific movement. Repeated-measures longitudinal study. Maximum isometric force and RFD at 50, 150, and 250 ms plus peak RFD were assessed for quadriceps and hamstrings. “Standard” asymmetry used the contemporaneous uninvolved limb; “real” asymmetry used its pre-ACLR value.
paper.tldr: This paper informs whether maximal force alone can conceal persistent rapid-force deficits after ACL reconstruction. Pre-ACLR quadriceps RFD asymmetry averaged 26% versus 14% for maximal force. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures longitudinal study. Maximum isometric force and RFD at 50, 150, and 250 ms plus peak RFD were assessed for quadriceps and hamstrings. “Standard” asymmetry used the contemporaneous uninvolved limb; “real” asymmetry used its pre-ACLR value.
paper.findings: Pre-ACLR quadriceps RFD asymmetry averaged 26% versus 14% for maximal force. At six months, “real” RFD asymmetries were 33–39% versus 26–28% using the contemporaneous uninvolved limb. Six-month involved-quadriceps RFD remained up to 14% below its pre-ACLR value even as maximal strength nearly recovered.
paper.limitations: Small heterogeneous male sample and uncontrolled pre-ACLR strength program. Single-joint isometric tests have uncertain ecological validity for high-velocity multijoint sport actions. Preoperative values are postinjury rather than true preinjury baselines. The study did not test whether RFD thresholds predict reinjury or safe return to sport.
paper.practicalImplications: Include rapid-force measures alongside maximal strength and absolute bilateral values, but do not interpret symmetry alone as readiness. When true preinjury baselines are unavailable, recognize that both the injured and comparison limb may change.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Include rapid-force measures alongside maximal strength and absolute bilateral values, but do not interpret symmetry alone as readiness. When true preinjury baselines are unavailable, recognize that both the injured and comparison limb may change. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, include rapid-force measures alongside maximal strength and absolute bilateral values, but do not interpret symmetry alone as readiness. When true preinjury baselines are unavailable, recognize that both the injured and comparison limb may change. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
